cells.tense: You are clearing the dead supports while the good ones hold.
cells.ask: Name the support you already tested and kept, and say why it stays.
cells.core:
You decide by what survives contact. You've sat with the same problem long enough that the answer got quiet and specific, and when something proves hollow you take it apart and move on. The clearing isn't a mood for you. It's what knowing what you're doing looks like from the outside.

That's the part worth noticing, because this kind of clearing rarely feels like a win. It feels like maintenance. But the ground you built on is solid because you checked it, not because you got lucky, and the people around you can stand on it. What gets free to feed what comes next is this: ground that's been tested can carry weight, so what do you put down there now?
cells.sheetLine: You keep what survives contact and you take apart the rest.
cells.verb: checking how a structure actually holds up, then deciding by what survives
cells.place: the moment a structure collapses because truth arrived

cells.tense: You will have cleared everything before anyone can question whether it needed clearing.
cells.ask: Pick one structure that's up and wait one week before touching it.
cells.core:
You're bracing for the collapse that hasn't come yet. Something tells you the room will fall, so you're already swinging — dismantling a thing that might be load-bearing, on the strength of a mood instead of evidence. The clearing is supposed to follow the truth arriving. Lately the clearing arrives first, and the truth is left to catch up.

If part of this holds through your week of waiting, you'll know because the thing failed on its own schedule, not yours, and not under your arm. What you'd lose either way is the habit of pre-grieving something that's holding. The clearing has its own timing. Your job is to have the evidence in hand before you touch the supports.
cells.sheetLine: You're tearing down walls before the news arrives. Let it arrive.

cells.tense: You stood at the door when the moment called and let it close behind you.
cells.ask: Say one thing plainly to someone today and leave it there without softening it.
cells.core:
The clearing hasn't happened lately. Something hollow is up, you can see it, and you haven't moved on it. Not because you can't tell the difference, but because a moment passed where it would have been easy, and you didn't step. The support stayed, the doubt stayed, and the room stayed the way it is.

The way back here isn't another round of thinking. It's contact: one honest exchange, where you say what the thing actually is and let the other person say something back. You don't need a plan to move. You need one sentence out loud, to a real person, and let the answer land on its own. Thinking about it more won't do what saying it once will.
cells.sheetLine: You know what's hollow. You haven't said so to anyone's face.

cells.tense: You are clearing the room and telling everyone the room cleared itself.
cells.ask: Point at one thing you took apart and say out loud that you did it.
cells.core:
You already did the clearing. You tested the claim, found it hollow, took the structure down — and then described it as the situation changing, people moving on, the thing falling apart by itself. The decision was yours. The story hands it to circumstance.

Modesty isn't the issue here. You're treating a choice you made as something that happened to you, and that leaves a piece of your own life outside your account of it. Underneath the habit there's usually an earlier form of the same thing: noticing, trying, being curious about what holds before you knew enough to dismantle anything with precision. The picture should include the hand that reached in and did it.
cells.sheetLine: You took it apart. The story says it fell.
